newsitem.title: GERMANY: German insurers face falling profits - study.
newsitem.headline: German insurers face falling profits - study.

text.p: German property and casualty insurers enjoyed "healthy profits" in 1996, but this was "with a high degree of probability the last year with a good profit for some time to come."
This is one of the findings of a major research project into German insurers' profitability undertaken by a group of Cologne insurance economists led by Professor Dieter Farny.

The study was published by "Versicherungswirtschaft" magazine, which has close ties with the industry. For the first time in four decades, German property and casualty insurers did not enjoy growth in 1996, the study says.

"Going by what we know now, the decreasing rates hit especially the large universal insurers, while the specialised motor insurers are less affected. Thus, the full consequences of this development cannot be judged yet," it adds.
Looking at the individual components of insurers' results, the economists came to the following conclusions for 1996:
- Overall, underwriting profits went down, although whether they slipped into the red cannot be said yet.

- Investment results were marked in 1996 by low interest rates for newly invested funds. Letting of property was difficult. There was little requirement to write down fixed-interest securities. "Strongly increased share prices allowed insurers to realise gains."

In 1997, German property-casualty insurers would suffer a dramatic decrease in motor premium income, the economists said. "The 'good' risks will pay markedly lower rates, while the 'bad' risks will avoid paying the higher levels," they noted.

"Motor insurers' new tariffs thus produce a special form of negative risk selection, a market-wide selection." The effect on individual companies depended on their portfolios and the way they managed the move from old to new motor tariffs.
The study said German insurers could cope with worsening results for some time. In 1995, the industry had achieved high profits, returning to the "remarkable" level of the late 1980s.
Real profitability was even higher than that publicly shown and the industry had "stored" some of the profits in order to sustain the lean years to come.
